was impossible to refuse. <break time="0.8s" /> Without explaining why. <break time="0.8s" /> So Waythorn found himself meeting. <break time="0.8s" /> His wifes second husband. <break time="0.8s" /> Regularly across the desk of his own office. <break time="0.8s" /> Varick behaved. <break time="0.8s" /> With easy good manners. <break time="0.8s" /> And Waythorn was forced to admit. <break time="0.8s" /> That the man was far easier to deal with than he had expected. <break time="0.8s" /> Meanwhile Haskett continued his visits. <break time="0.8s" /> To his recovering daughter. <break time="0.8s" /> And one afternoon. <break time="0.8s" /> Coming home early. <break time="0.8s" /> Waythorn found him waiting alone. <break time="0.8s" /> In the library of his own house. <break time="0.8s" /> He was a small, effaced looking man. <break time="0.8s" /> With a thin gray beard. <break time="0.8s" /> Whose shabby respectability. <break time="0.8s" /> Made it hard to believe. <break time="0.8s" /> That Alice had once been his wife. <break time="0.8s" /> Waythorns eye was caught by his tie. <break time="0.8s" /> A made up tie fastened with an elastic. <break time="0.8s" /> And that small detail. <break time="0.8s" /> Seemed to tell the whole story of Hasketts life. <break time="0.8s" /> He suddenly pictured Alice. <break time="0.8s" /> As Missus Haskett. <break time="0.8s" /> Sitting in a plush furnished front parlor in Utica. <break time="0.8s" /> And pushing a baby carriage along the street. <break time="0.8s" /> On Sunday afternoons. <break time="0.8s" /> The picture troubled him deeply. <break time="0.8s" /> For if she had once fitted so easily. <break time="0.8s" /> Into that life. <break time="0.8s" /> How many other lives might she have fitted into just as easily. <break time="0.8s" /> Had he known how lightly. <break time="0.8s" /> She could put aside her past. <break time="0.8s" /> He might never have felt so secure. <break time="0.8s" /> In the life they were beginning together.
